title: Liber contra Joan. Hierosolymitanum
author: Jerome
source: Translated by Claude from tmp423.tmp423.opp-lat1, as held by Open Greek and Latin's Patrologia Latina.
statement: An AI-generated translation. No specialist has reviewed it.

passages.original: -Quaerimus utrum animae antequam homo in paradiso fieret, et plasmaretur Adam de terra, inter rationabiles fuerint creaturas; utrum proprium statum habuerint, vixerint, mo- ratae sint, atque substiterint, et an Origenis do- ctrina sit vera, qui dixit cunctas rationabiles crea- turas, incorporales et invisibiles, si negligentiores fuerint, paulatim ad inferiora labi, et juxta qua- litates locorum ad quae defluunt, assumere sihi corpora. Verbi gratia, primum aetherea, deinde aerea.
passages.english: We ask whether souls, before man was made in paradise and Adam was formed from the earth, existed among the rational creatures; whether they had a state of their own, lived, dwelt, and subsisted; and whether the teaching of Origen is true, who said that all rational creatures, incorporeal and invisible, if they became more negligent, slip little by little to lower [levels], and according to the qualities of the places to which they flow down, take bodies on themselves: for example, first ethereal, then aerial.

passages.original: 17. Quid in librisπ*ρ\'Αρχώνdicebat Origenes. Quo tempore Commentarios edidit in Ecclesiasten Hieronymus. — Credis quod cunctas visibiles et invisibiles creaturas unus Deus fecerit : hoc et Arius confiteretur, qui dicit cuncta creata per Fi- lium. Si de Marcionis arguereris haeresi, quae alte- rum bonum, alterum justum Deum inferens 2, illum invisibilium, hunc visibilium asserit Creato- rem, recte mihi de hujusmodi satisfeceris quaestio- ne.
passages.english: 17. What Origen said in the books *Peri Archōn* [On First Principles]. At the time when Jerome published his Commentaries on Ecclesiastes. — You believe that one God made all creatures visible and invisible: even Arius would confess this, who says that all things were created through the Son. If you were being charged with the heresy of Marcion, which, introducing one God [who is] good and another [who is] just, asserts that the former is Creator of things invisible and the latter of things visible, you would rightly have satisfied me on a question of this kind.
passages.notes: The Greek title is garbled in the scan ("π*ρ\'Αρχών"); read as Περὶ Ἀρχῶν. The '2' after 'inferens' is a footnote mark, omitted. The second sentence of the heading is obscure as transmitted; it appears to be an editorial heading or gloss rather than part of the argument.

passages.original: sed ante primicerius, deinde senator 11, ducenarius, centenarius, 425 biarchus, circitor, eques, dein tiro; et quanquam tribunus quondam miles gregarius sit, tamen ex tribuno non tiro, sed primicerius factus est. Docet Origenes per scalam Jacob paulatim rationabiles creaturas ad ultimum gradum, id est, ad carnem et sanguinem descen- dere : nec fieri posse, ut de centenario numero su- bito quis ad unum numerum praecipitetur, nisi per singulos numeros, quasi per scalae gradus, ad ulti- mum usque perveniat;
passages.english: but first a primicerius, then a senator, ducenarius, centenarius, biarchus, circitor, cavalryman, then recruit; and although a tribune was once a common soldier, yet from tribune he was made not a recruit but a primicerius. Origen teaches that by Jacob's ladder rational creatures descend little by little to the last rung, that is, to flesh and blood; and that it cannot happen that someone is thrown down suddenly from the number one hundred to the number one, unless he arrives at the last through each single number, as though through the rungs of a ladder;
passages.notes: The ranks (primicerius, senator, ducenarius, centenarius, biarchus, circitor) are late Roman military grades in descending order, kept untranslated. The numeral 425 is a page marker, omitted.

passages.original: et tamen antequam vultum draconis evolvam, et dogma Origenis de resurre- ctione breviter exponam (non enim poteris vim scire antidoti, nisi venena perspexeris), illud dili- genter observa et caute relegens numera : quod no- vies resurrectionem nominans corporis, ne semel quidem carnis inseruit : suspectumque tibi sit, quod de industria praetermisit. Dicit ergo Origenes 431 in pluribus locis, et maxime in libro de Re- surrectione quarto, et in Expositione primi psalmi, et in Stromatibus, duplicem errorem versari in Ec- clesia; nostrorum et haereticorum : « Nos simpli- ces et philosarcas 6 dicere, quod eadem ossa, et sanguis, et caro, id est, vultus et membra, totius- que compago corporis resurgat in novissima die : scilicet ut pedibus ambulemus, operemur manibus, videamus oculis, auribus audiamus, circum fera- musque ventrem insatiabilem, et stomachum cibos concoquentem.
passages.english: and yet, before I unroll the dragon's face and briefly set out Origen's doctrine on the resurrection (for you cannot know the power of the antidote unless you have examined the poisons), observe this carefully and count as you cautiously reread: that, naming the resurrection of the body nine times, he did not once insert [the resurrection] of the flesh; and let what he deliberately passed over be suspect to you. Origen, then, says in many places, and especially in the fourth book On the Resurrection, and in the Exposition of the first Psalm, and in the Stromateis, that a twofold error is current in the Church, ours and the heretics': "We simple folk and flesh-lovers say that the same bones and blood and flesh, that is, face and limbs and the whole structure of the body, rise again on the last day: namely, so that we may walk with feet, work with hands, see with eyes, hear with ears, and carry around an insatiable belly and a stomach digesting food.
passages.notes: "philosarcas" (Greek philosarkoi, 'flesh-lovers'). The numeral 431 and footnote mark 6 omitted.

passages.original: Quod autem ab oculis repente evanuit, virtus Dei est, non umbrae et phantasmatis. Alioquin et ante resurrectionem, cum eduxissent eum de Naza- reth, ut praecipitarent de supercilio montis, trans- ivit per medios, id est, elapsus est de manibus eo- rum. Nunquid juxta Marcionem dicere possumus, quod ideo nativitas ejus in phantasmate fuerit, quia contra naturam qui tenebatur, elapsus est? Quod magis licet, hoc Domino non licet? Apollo- nius Tyaneus scribitur cum ante Domitianum staret in consistorio, repente non comparuisse.
passages.english: But that he suddenly vanished from their eyes is the power of God, not of a shadow and a phantom. Otherwise, even before the resurrection, when they had led him out of Nazareth to throw him down from the brow of the hill, he passed through the midst of them, that is, he slipped out of their hands. Can we say, with Marcion, that his birth was therefore in phantom form, because he who was being held slipped away contrary to nature? Is what is permitted to magicians not permitted to the Lord? Apollonius of Tyana is recorded to have suddenly disappeared when he was standing before Domitian in the council chamber.
passages.notes: 'Quod magis licet' is evidently a scanning error for 'Quod magis licet' → 'Quod magis [magis = magicians] licet', i.e. 'magis' read as dative of 'magi' (cf. 'magorum praestigiis' in the following context); translated accordingly.
